title: Design Patterns in the Wild
tagline: You already use design patterns every day — Express middleware, Redux actions, React HOCs, Node streams. This lesson names what you've been doing and shows the structural DNA behind each tool.

sections.content:
Design patterns are not academic inventions reserved for enterprise Java architects. They are the *invisible skeleton* inside the tools you ship code with every day. Express middleware is **Chain of Responsibility**. Redux is a triad of **Observer**, **Command**, and **Singleton**. React component trees are **Composite**. Higher-Order Components are **Decorator**. Node.js `Transform` streams are **Decorator** layered on **Adapter**. A JavaScript `Promise` is a **State Machine**. ORM query builders are **Builder**.

The GoF (Gang of Four) book, published in 1994, documented 23 patterns by observing recurring structures in successful object-oriented codebases. Thirty years later, those same structures reappear in functional JavaScript, TypeScript, and modern frameworks — just wearing different clothes. The vocabulary has not aged; only the syntax has changed.

Learning to see the pattern beneath the API pays two concrete dividends. First, you read unfamiliar libraries dramatically faster — when you open Fastify's source code and see middleware composition, you immediately recognise it as Chain of Responsibility and already know how error propagation works. Second, you design your own abstractions with the confidence of a proven blueprint rather than improvising from scratch. This lesson walks through six real tools, deconstructs the code you already write, and names the pattern hiding inside each one. We will also cover the *problems* each pattern solves, the classic UML participants, before-and-after code showing why the pattern exists, and the edge cases where it breaks down.

sections.title: An Airport and a Newspaper: Two Patterns from Daily Life
sections.content:
Picture airport security: you pass through document check → X-ray → body scanner → customs declaration. Each station handles its single concern and passes you to the next — or stops you cold if something is wrong. You (the `request`) do not choose the order. The airport authority (the `app`) configures the sequence before you arrive. A single station can short-circuit the rest — document check can turn you away before you ever reach the X-ray. That is **Chain of Responsibility** — exactly what `app.use(fn)` does in Express. The chain is assembled once at startup; requests flow through it at runtime.

Now think of a **newspaper subscription service**. The newspaper office (the Redux store) holds the current edition (state). Subscribers (React components) register their interest once (`store.subscribe`). Every time a new edition is printed (`dispatch(action)`) — regardless of whether the subscriber was online when it was sent — every subscriber is notified with the latest edition. The office does not need to know what each subscriber does with the paper. That is **Observer**: a one-to-many dependency where subjects notify dependents automatically.

The action itself — `{ type: 'ADD_ITEM', payload: { id: 42 } }` — is the *print order*, not the printed paper. It is a serialisable record of intent. The editor (reducer) receives the order and decides what the new edition looks like. That is **Command**: encapsulate a request as a data object so you can queue it, log it, replay it, or undo it. Redux DevTools' time-travel feature exists *because* actions are Commands — you can re-run the command log from any point in history.

sections.title: Chain of Responsibility — Express and Koa Middleware
sections.content:
**The problem it solves:** You have a sequence of processing steps (logging, authentication, rate-limiting, parsing, business logic, error handling) that must run in a specific order on every incoming request. Hardcoding all these concerns into a single function produces an unmaintainable monolith. Each concern needs to be independently testable, reorderable, and optionally removable.

**The pattern:** Create a chain of handler objects. Each handler decides to (a) handle the request and terminate, (b) pass to the next handler, or (c) handle the request and *also* pass to the next. Handlers do not know about each other — they only know about `next`.

**Participants in Express:** The `app` object is the *chain manager*. Each `app.use(fn)` call appends a handler to an internal array. When a request arrives, Express calls handlers in registration order, threading `req`, `res`, and `next` through each. A handler that calls `next(err)` with an argument bypasses normal handlers and jumps to the nearest four-argument error handler `(err, req, res, next)`.

**Koa's Onion Model — Chain of Responsibility + Decorator:** Koa's `compose(middlewares)` function wraps each middleware around the remaining stack, creating a concentric onion. `await next()` suspends the current middleware, runs everything inside it, then resumes. This means outer middleware runs *before and after* inner middleware — a classic Decorator wrapping. Express cannot do this without callbacks; Koa's async/await makes it natural.

**The before-after contrast:** Without the pattern you write one enormous function. With Chain of Responsibility you write narrow, testable handlers that can be unit-tested in isolation by calling them with mock `req`, `res`, and `next`.

sections.mermaid:
flowchart LR
    Req["HTTP Request"] --> L["Logger\nmiddleware"]
    L -->|"next()"| A["Auth\nmiddleware"]
    A -->|"next()"| R["Rate limiter\nmiddleware"]
    R -->|"next()"| H["Route handler"]
    H --> Res["HTTP Response"]
    A -->|"401 — chain stops"| Res
sections.caption: Each middleware is a link. Auth can terminate the chain early (401) without the route handler ever executing. Logger always calls next() — it is a pure pass-through observer.

sections.label: Example
sections.explanation: The 'before' version violates single-responsibility and is nearly impossible to unit test. The 'after' splits each concern into a handler that can be tested by calling it directly with mocked req/res/next. Koa's await next() adds the Decorator ability to act both before and after the inner chain — essential for timing, transaction wrapping, and error handling that needs to clean up after child handlers.

sections.title: Command + Observer + Singleton — Redux
sections.content:
**The problem it solves:** Multiple UI components need to share and react to the same state. Without a central store, components pass props down many layers (prop drilling), siblings cannot communicate directly, and state becomes fragmented across local component state. Testing is difficult because state is tied to component lifecycle.

**Three patterns in one `createStore` call:**

**Singleton** — `createStore` returns a single store object. The store is imported by name anywhere in the app. All components talk to the same instance. This is classic Singleton: ensure a class has exactly one instance and provide a global access point to it. Caveat: Redux's store is not enforced at the language level — you *could* call `createStore` twice. The convention enforces the singleton.

**Command** — Every `dispatch({ type: 'ADD_ITEM', payload: { id: 42 } })` sends a Command object: a serialisable data record that *describes intent* without executing it. The reducer is the Command's executor (the *invoker* in GoF terms). Because commands are plain objects, they can be serialised to JSON, logged to a database, replayed in any order, and diffed. Redux DevTools' time-travel debugging is a direct consequence — it literally re-runs the command log from an initial snapshot.

**Observer** — `store.subscribe(listener)` registers a callback. After every dispatch, Redux calls every registered listener. Listeners do not know what caused the dispatch; they just know state changed. `react-redux`'s `connect()` and `useSelector` hooks implement the Observer registration under the hood, triggering re-renders only when the relevant slice of state changes.

**The before-after contrast:** Without these patterns you pass `setState` callbacks five levels down (Command without serialisation) or use global variables (Singleton without the contract). With Redux, the data flow is strictly one-directional and entirely inspectable.

sections.mermaid:
sequenceDiagram
    participant UI as "React Component"
    participant S as "Redux Store (Singleton)"
    participant R as "Reducer (Command Executor)"
    participant Sub as "Subscriber (Observer)"
    UI->>S: dispatch({ type: 'INCREMENT', by: 1 })
    Note over S: Command received
    S->>R: (currentState, action)
    R-->>S: nextState
    Note over S: State updated
    S->>Sub: notify all listeners
    Sub-->>UI: component re-renders with new state
sections.caption: Redux data flow: the dispatched action is a Command, the store applies it via the reducer (Command executor), then notifies all subscribers via Observer. The store itself is a Singleton — the same object reference is used throughout the app.

sections.label: Example
sections.explanation: The createStore implementation in ~25 lines makes all three patterns visible. The subscriber array is the Observer registry. dispatch accepts only plain objects (Command objects must be serialisable). getState returning state by reference (not a copy) is a deliberate Redux decision — components that mutate state directly break the pattern because reducers would not produce new references and subscriber notifications would be missed.

sections.title: Decorator + Composite + Strategy — React
sections.content:
**The problem Composite solves:** You need a tree of UI elements where parent and leaf nodes must be treated uniformly. A `<Page>` contains `<Section>` which contains `<Button>` — but React's reconciler should not need special cases for leaves vs branches. Both must implement the same interface (`render` / function component signature), so the reconciler can traverse the tree recursively without knowing whether a node has children.

**Composite in React:** Every component — leaf or branch — is a function (or class) that receives props and returns JSX. The reconciler calls each node the same way. A `<Button>` with no children and a `<Grid>` with forty children are structurally identical from the reconciler's perspective. This uniformity is the essence of Composite.

**The problem Decorator solves:** You want to add cross-cutting concerns (authentication checks, analytics tracking, loading spinners, error boundaries) to a component without modifying its source code. You want the enhancement to be composable and removable.

**Decorator via Higher-Order Components:** `withAuth(Dashboard)` returns a new component that wraps `Dashboard`. The HOC renders the child if authenticated, or redirects otherwise. The `Dashboard` component has no auth logic — it does one thing. Multiple decorators compose: `withLogging(withAuth(withErrorBoundary(Dashboard)))`. The prop interface remains the same (pass-through props). This is textbook Decorator: add behaviour by wrapping, not by modifying.

**React hooks replaced HOCs for most uses** — `useAuth()`, `useAnalytics()` — but the pattern is the same idea in functional form. The wrapping is now implicit (hook called inside the component body) rather than explicit (HOC wrapping at import).

**Strategy via render props:** `<DataFetcher url='/api/users' render={data => <Table rows={data} />} />` injects the *rendering algorithm* as a prop. The `DataFetcher` owns the data-fetching logic; the caller owns the rendering logic. Swapping the `render` prop changes the output without touching `DataFetcher`. Children-as-functions (`children(data)`) is the same pattern by a different name.

sections.caption: Composite: LeafButton and BranchSection both implement Component. HOCDecorator also implements Component (same interface) while wrapping another Component — Decorator reusing the Composite interface.

sections.title: Decorator + Adapter — Node.js Streams
sections.content:
**The problem Adapter solves:** File systems, HTTP connections, TCP sockets, and in-memory buffers all produce or consume data, but each has a completely different API. You cannot `pipe` a raw TCP socket directly to a file without a translation layer. Node.js streams define a common `Readable`/`Writable` interface and implement it for every data source. The stream is an Adapter: it converts a source-specific API into the universal streaming contract.

**The problem Decorator solves (stream layers):** You want to add behaviour to a data stream — compress it, encrypt it, split lines, parse JSON — without the data source knowing or caring. Each transformation should be stackable.

**Node streams as Decorator chains:** `Transform` streams implement both `Readable` and `Writable`. Each `.pipe(transform)` adds a layer of behaviour while preserving the same `pipe`-able interface. The source emits chunks; the Transform receives them, transforms them, and re-emits. The sink receives the final transformed chunks. The source does not know it is being compressed; the sink does not know the source is a file.

```
fs.createReadStream(src)       // Adapter: file → Readable
  .pipe(zlib.createGzip())     // Decorator: add compression
  .pipe(crypto.createCipher()) // Decorator: add encryption
  .pipe(fs.createWriteStream(dst)) // Adapter: Writable → file
```

This composes three independent behaviours. Swapping `zlib.createGzip()` for `zlib.createDeflate()` changes the algorithm without touching any other layer. Adding a progress-tracking Transform in the middle requires no changes to source or sink. This composability is the Decorator pattern's central promise.

**The backpressure mechanism** is baked into the interface. When the sink is slow, `pipe` automatically pauses the source. Every layer honours this — another benefit of the uniform Adapter interface.

flowchart LR

    B -->|"compressed chunks"| C["crypto.createCipher\nDecorator: encrypt"]
    C -->|"encrypted chunks"| D["fs.createWriteStream\nAdapter: Writable -> file"]
    style A fill:#d4edda
    style B fill:#cce5ff
    style C fill:#cce5ff
    style D fill:#d4edda
sections.caption: Green nodes are Adapters (translating OS APIs to the stream interface). Blue nodes are Decorators (adding behaviour while preserving the interface). Each pipe call adds a layer without touching adjacent layers.

sections.title: State Machine — JavaScript Promises
sections.content:
**The problem it solves:** Asynchronous operations have lifecycle phases — in-progress, succeeded, failed. Without a formal state model, you write ad-hoc boolean flags (`isLoading`, `isError`, `isDone`), which can legally represent impossible combinations like `isLoading: true, isDone: true`. A state machine eliminates impossible states by design.

**Promise as a 3-state FSM:** A Promise starts in `pending`. A call to `resolve(value)` transitions it to `fulfilled` with the resolved value. A call to `reject(reason)` transitions it to `rejected` with the rejection reason. `fulfilled` and `rejected` are terminal states — once reached, no further transitions occur.

**Why termination matters:** Calling `resolve()` twice on the same promise is silently ignored — the state machine is already in a terminal state. This prevents a whole class of bugs where multiple async callbacks accidentally settle the same promise multiple times (race conditions in network retry logic, for example).

**The state transition rules:**
- `pending → fulfilled` (via `resolve`): irreversible
- `pending → rejected` (via `reject`): irreversible
- `fulfilled → anything`: impossible
- `rejected → anything`: impossible

**Promise chaining creates a new machine:** `.then(fn)` returns a *new* Promise in `pending`. It transitions based on whether `fn` throws (rejected) or returns normally (fulfilled). The chain is a pipeline of state machines, not a single machine with more states.

**This insight explains several 'quirks':** Why does `Promise.resolve(42).then(v => v * 2)` return a new Promise rather than 84? Because each `.then` is a new state machine. Why does throwing inside `.then` cause a rejection rather than an uncaught error? Because the catch arm of the new machine intercepts it. Why can you not cancel a Promise? Because there is no transition from `fulfilled` or `pending` back to `pending` — the FSM has no backward edges.

sections.mermaid:
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> Pending
    Pending --> Fulfilled : resolve(value)
    Pending --> Rejected : reject(reason)
    Fulfilled --> [*]
    Rejected --> [*]
sections.caption: The Promise state machine: three states, two transition triggers, two terminal states. No backward edges — transitions are strictly one-directional. This is why calling resolve() twice is safe (the second call is a no-op).

sections.title: Builder Pattern — ORM Query Builders
sections.content:
**The problem it solves:** Constructing complex SQL queries with many optional parts (joins, where clauses, ordering, pagination, eager loading) using string concatenation produces fragile, injection-prone, unreadable code. The query is not valid until all parts are assembled — you cannot execute a half-built query. You need a way to accumulate parameters incrementally and only execute when explicitly told to.

**The pattern:** Separate the construction of a complex object from its representation. A Builder object accumulates configuration through a fluent API (each method returns `this`). The final `build()` / `getMany()` / `execute()` call converts the accumulated state into the target object (SQL string, HTTP request, DOM element).

**Participants in TypeORM:** `createQueryBuilder('user')` creates the builder. `.where('user.active = :active', { active: true })` adds a condition. `.leftJoinAndSelect('user.orders', 'order')` adds a join. `.orderBy('user.createdAt', 'DESC')` sets ordering. `.take(10).skip(20)` sets pagination. `.getMany()` is the *director* step that compiles the accumulated state into SQL and executes it.

**Why fluent interfaces are not always Builder:** A fluent interface (method chaining) is a *syntax choice*. Builder is a *design pattern*. Moment.js `moment().add(1, 'day').format('YYYY-MM-DD')` is fluent but is not Builder because `moment()` constructs an already-valid object, not an under-construction one. True Builder: the object under construction is invalid/unusable until `build()` is called.

**Active Record vs. Builder in ORMs:** Sequelize model instances (`.save()`, `.destroy()`) are **Active Record** — the domain object knows how to persist itself. TypeORM's `QueryBuilder` is pure **Builder** — it constructs a query specification, not a domain object. Most ORMs offer both patterns simultaneously.

sections.label: Example
sections.explanation: The Builder separates construction from execution. Each layer of the application (service, controller, business logic) contributes to the query without executing it prematurely. Parameterisation happens inside the Builder — no layer can accidentally inject raw values. The build() method is the only place SQL is assembled, making it trivial to add query logging, caching, or validation in one place.

sections.title: When to Use Each Pattern — and When NOT To
sections.content:
**Chain of Responsibility — use when:**
- You have a sequence of handlers and the sender should not need to know which handler will ultimately process the request.
- You want to add/remove handlers at runtime without changing the sender.
- Handlers must be independently testable (logging, auth, rate-limiting).

**Do NOT use Chain of Responsibility when:** the chain will almost always be length 1 (just call the function directly), or when the caller *must* know which handler processed the request (use a map-dispatch instead).

**Command — use when:**
- You need to log, queue, replay, or undo operations.
- You want to decouple the sender of a request from its executor.
- Operations need to be serialised across a network or to disk.

**Do NOT use Command** for simple synchronous operations where the overhead of an object per operation is not justified. A `setTimeout(fn, delay)` is already decoupled — wrapping it in a Command class adds ceremony without benefit.

**Observer — use when:**
- Multiple objects need to react to state changes in another object.
- The subject should not know which objects subscribe to it.
- You expect a variable number of dependents.

**Do NOT use Observer** when the relationship is one-to-one and stable — just call the function directly. Excessive Observer usage creates invisible data flows that are hard to trace in debugging (the 'spooky action at a distance' problem). Every `.subscribe()` that is never `.unsubscribe()`'d is a memory leak.

**Decorator — use when:**
- You need to add behaviour to individual objects without affecting others of the same class.
- You need composable, mix-and-match enhancements.
- Subclassing would produce a combinatorial explosion of classes.

**Do NOT use Decorator** when you need to change the interface — Decorator preserves the interface. If you need a fundamentally different API, use Adapter. Do not stack more than 3-4 decorators — deep wrapping makes stack traces unreadable.

**Builder — use when:**
- Object construction requires many optional parameters.
- The object is invalid in partially-constructed states.
- The same construction process should create different representations.

**Do NOT use Builder** for objects with 1-3 parameters — a simple constructor or object literal is clearer. Builder adds indirection; reserve it for genuinely complex construction.

**State Machine — use when:**
- An object's behaviour depends on its state, and it transitions between states at defined points.
- You want to make illegal states unrepresentable.

**Do NOT use State Machine** for simple boolean flags. If an object truly has only two states and one transition, a boolean is correct. State machines shine when there are 3+ states with non-trivial transition rules.

sections.title: Common Misconceptions About Design Patterns
sections.content:
**'Patterns are object-oriented only':** The GoF book used Java/C++ examples, but the underlying *structural problems* exist in any paradigm. Functional composition (`pipe(fn1, fn2, fn3)`) is Chain of Responsibility. Closures that maintain private state and expose a public API are Singleton. Currying is a form of Builder — accumulating arguments before execution. The names and vocabulary apply across paradigms.

**'Patterns are always the right solution':** Patterns are solutions to recurring problems *in specific contexts*. Applying a pattern where the problem does not exist is over-engineering. The Single Responsibility Principle matters more than pattern coverage — prefer a simple function over a Command object unless you actually need queueing, replaying, or undoing.

**'HOCs are deprecated by hooks':** React hooks replaced HOCs for *most* use cases, but HOCs are not Decorator-pattern-deprecated — the Decorator structure is still correct for class components, for wrapping third-party components you cannot modify, and for situations where the enhancement must be applied at the module boundary rather than inside the function body.

**'Observer and Event Emitter are different things':** Node.js `EventEmitter` is Observer with topic routing. `emitter.on('data', fn)` is `subject.subscribe(fn)` with a topic key. The structural relationship is identical — EventEmitter is Observer specialised for named event channels.

**'The Singleton pattern is always bad':** Singletons are problematic when they carry mutable shared state that makes testing unpredictable. Redux's store is a Singleton but is designed to be easily swapped in tests by calling `createStore` again. A Singleton that holds immutable configuration is completely safe. The problem is not Singleton per se — it is mutable global state.

sections.title: Real Frameworks and Where Each Pattern Lives
sections.content:
Understanding which patterns a framework is built on tells you *why* its API is shaped the way it is, and predicts how it will behave in edge cases.

**Express / Fastify / Koa:** Chain of Responsibility is the core architecture. Fastify extends it with a plugin system (**Decorator** + **Facade**) that encapsulates groups of routes and middleware. Koa's `compose` is a textbook implementation of both Chain of Responsibility and Decorator.

**Redux / Zustand / Jotai:** Redux = Singleton + Command + Observer as described. Zustand simplifies to Singleton + Observer (mutations are direct function calls, not Command objects — so no time-travel). Jotai uses **Atom** pattern (a variant of Observer where each atom is a mini-subject).

**React / Vue / Svelte:** Component trees are always Composite. React HOCs are Decorator; Vue mixins are a weaker Decorator. Vue's `provide/inject` and React's `Context` are **Mediator** — a central hub decouples producers from consumers. Svelte stores are Observer.

**TypeORM / Prisma / Sequelize:** QueryBuilder is Builder. Model instances are Active Record (a combination of **Domain Object** and **Data Mapper**). Prisma's middleware system (`prisma.$use(fn)`) is Chain of Responsibility.

**RxJS:** Observables are Observer pattern taken to its logical extreme — every value in a stream is a notification. `pipe(map(...), filter(...), debounceTime(...))` is a Decorator chain (each operator wraps the stream). `switchMap`, `mergeMap`, `concatMap` are **Strategy** — different concurrency algorithms for inner observables.

**NestJS:** Uses **Decorator** (TypeScript class decorators: `@Controller`, `@Injectable`, `@Get`) for metadata annotation. Dependency injection is **Service Locator** or **IoC Container** (an inversion of the Factory pattern). Guards and Interceptors are Chain of Responsibility wired by the framework.

**Historical context:** The Gang of Four (Erich Gamma, Richard Helm, Ralph Johnson, John Vlissides) published *Design Patterns: Elements of Reusable Object-Oriented Software* in 1994. They explicitly acknowledged that the patterns they documented were *observations*, not inventions — recurring solutions that skilled programmers had independently discovered. The book's contribution was naming and cataloguing them so the community could communicate about them precisely. The same principle holds today: when you call something 'Builder' in a code review, every engineer on the team immediately understands the construction-separation intent without reading the implementation.

**Pattern-spotting shortcut — three diagnostic questions:** When you encounter an unfamiliar API, ask: (1) Does it chain calls and pass control to the next handler? **Chain of Responsibility**. (2) Does it let you subscribe/observe state changes that happen elsewhere? **Observer**. (3) Does it wrap an object to add behaviour while preserving its interface? **Decorator**. These three patterns alone cover roughly 70% of common JavaScript library designs. A second tier: (4) Does it accumulate parameters before executing? **Builder**. (5) Does it describe intent as a data object rather than a direct call? **Command**. (6) Does it enforce that only specific transitions between states are possible? **State Machine**. With these six questions you can classify the structural DNA of almost any API you encounter.

items: **Express / Koa middleware** is **Chain of Responsibility**: each handler decides to continue (`next()`) or terminate — Koa adds a **Decorator** onion with `await next()` so outer middleware can act both before and after the inner stack.

**Redux** combines three patterns in one API: **Singleton** store (single source of truth), **Command** action objects (serialisable, replayable, loggable), and **Observer** subscribers notified after every dispatch — time-travel debugging is a direct consequence of the Command pattern.

**React** uses **Composite** for its component tree (leaves and branches share the same interface), **Decorator** for HOCs (wrapping without modifying), and **Strategy** for render props (swappable rendering algorithm passed as a parameter).

**Node.js streams** are **Decorator** chains (each `pipe` adds behaviour) built on an **Adapter** interface that normalises files, sockets, and HTTP into a single `pipe`-able contract with built-in backpressure.

**ORM query builders** are **Builder** pattern: fluent chaining accumulates parameters in an invalid intermediate state before `build()` / `getMany()` executes — preventing partially-constructed invalid queries and enabling injection-safe parameterisation.

**Promises** are **State Machines** with three states (pending, fulfilled, rejected) and two irreversible terminal transitions — calling `resolve()` twice is safe precisely because the state machine has no transition from a terminal state.

Naming the pattern you are implementing in code reviews, documentation, and architecture discussions is not jargon — it is precision: a single word replaces a paragraph of explanation and immediately aligns the entire team's mental model.

quiz.question: Express `app.use((req, res, next) => { next() })` implements which pattern, and what is the key structural clue?
options: Observer — the handler subscribes to incoming request events
Chain of Responsibility — each handler passes control to the next via next(), and can terminate the chain early
Command — the handler encapsulates the request as a serialisable object
Decorator — the handler wraps res to add logging behaviour
quiz.explanation: Chain of Responsibility: each middleware is a link. The structural clue is the next() parameter — calling it delegates to the next link. Omitting it terminates the chain. The chain is assembled by app.use calls in registration order; handlers do not reference each other directly.

quiz.question: Why is a Redux action object `{ type: 'ADD_ITEM', payload: { id: 42 } }` classified as a Command pattern rather than a simple function call?
options: Because it is dispatched asynchronously through a Promise
Because it is a serialisable data record describing intent — it can be logged, queued, replayed, and undone without re-executing the original caller
Because it is the only mechanism that can modify the Redux store
Because it triggers Observer notifications to all subscribers
quiz.explanation: Command pattern: the action is a plain serialisable object (describable as JSON) that encodes *what should happen*, not *how*. The reducer executes the intent later. This decoupling is why Redux DevTools can replay history — it re-runs the command log against an initial snapshot.

quiz.question: What makes `withAuth(Dashboard)` a Decorator rather than a Factory?
options: It creates a new component class — that is exactly what Factory does, so they are interchangeable
It wraps Dashboard to add authentication behaviour while preserving the same component interface — callers cannot tell it is wrapped
It assembles a complex component from many parts, like a Builder
It subscribes Dashboard to auth state changes, making it an Observer
quiz.explanation: Decorator: withAuth returns a new component that implements the same interface as Dashboard (receives the same props, returns JSX). The key is interface preservation — the caller treats the wrapped component identically to the original. A Factory would create an object without requiring the same interface as its input.

quiz.question: `fs.createReadStream().pipe(zlib.createGzip()).pipe(dest)` uses Decorator. What specific property of each Transform stream enables this pattern?
options: Each Transform is a Singleton — there is only one instance per process
Each Transform implements both Readable and Writable, preserving the pipe-able interface so any Transform can wrap any other
Each Transform uses Chain of Responsibility to decide whether to pass chunks downstream
Each Transform stores chunks as Command objects before flushing
quiz.explanation: Decorator requires interface preservation. A Node.js Transform implements both Readable and Writable, so it can receive data from a Readable upstream and expose data to a Writable downstream — the same interface in and out. This is what allows arbitrary stacking: any Transform can wrap any other without breaking the chain.

quiz.question: A Promise that has resolved to 'done' is called with `resolve('other')` a second time. What happens, and which aspect of the State Machine pattern explains it?
options: The Promise rejects — double resolution is an error
The Promise value updates to 'other' — the latest resolve wins
Nothing — fulfilled is a terminal state with no outgoing transitions, so the second call is silently ignored
A second .then() chain begins from the new value
quiz.explanation: State Machine: fulfilled and rejected are terminal states — the FSM has no outgoing transitions from them. Once in a terminal state, resolve() and reject() calls are no-ops. This is not a bug or oversight; it is a deliberate design choice that prevents race conditions where multiple async callbacks try to settle the same Promise.

quiz.question: TypeORM's `createQueryBuilder('user').where(...).leftJoinAndSelect(...).take(10).getMany()` is Builder. What is the key property that distinguishes Builder from a simple fluent interface?
options: Builder methods must return new objects, never this
The object under construction is invalid or unusable until the terminal step (getMany) is called — intermediate states are incomplete
Builder requires a separate Director class to orchestrate construction
Fluent interfaces always build strings, while Builder always builds objects
quiz.explanation: The defining characteristic of Builder is that the object under construction is in an invalid intermediate state until build() / getMany() is called. A fluent interface is a syntax choice (method chaining that returns this); Builder is a structural pattern where the product cannot be used until fully assembled. Not every fluent interface is a Builder.

quiz.question: React's component tree where `<Page>` contains `<Section>` which contains `<Button>` implements Composite. What is the critical structural requirement that Composite enforces?
options: All components must extend a base class with a render method
Leaf nodes (Button) and branch nodes (Page, Section) must implement the same interface so the reconciler can traverse the tree uniformly without special-casing
Components must be arranged in a strict two-level hierarchy
Only leaf nodes can receive props — branch nodes pass them down automatically
quiz.explanation: Composite's defining requirement is uniform interface across leaves and branches. React's reconciler calls every component — Button, Section, Page — the same way (pass props, receive JSX). It does not need to check whether a node has children before recursing. This uniformity is what makes recursive tree traversal simple and extensible.

quiz.question: Koa's middleware uses `await next()` so outer middleware can run code *after* the inner chain completes. Which pattern does this onion model add beyond basic Chain of Responsibility?
options: Singleton — a single composed middleware function runs the whole stack
Decorator — each middleware wraps the remaining stack, adding behaviour both before (pre-next) and after (post-next) the inner handlers
Command — next() stores the remaining chain as a replayable object
Strategy — each middleware selects a different algorithm for processing the request
quiz.explanation: Decorator: await next() suspends the current middleware and resumes after the inner stack completes. Code before next() runs on the way in; code after next() runs on the way out. This wrapping structure — where each layer surrounds the layers inside it — is classic Decorator, used for timing, transaction wrapping, and response post-processing.

quiz.question: Which real-world scenario is the Command pattern's serialisability MOST critical for?
options: Synchronous validation of form fields before submission
Routing HTTP requests to the correct controller method
Redux DevTools time-travel debugging — re-running a log of past actions against an initial state snapshot
React reconciliation of virtual DOM trees
quiz.explanation: Time-travel debugging requires replaying operations in any order from any point in history. This is only possible if operations are serialisable data objects (Commands) rather than direct function calls. Redux stores every dispatched action; DevTools replays the action log against a snapshot state to reconstruct any historical state.

quiz.question: You are designing a notification service where multiple UI components (badge count, toast, audio alert) react to a single 'new message' event. The components are added and removed dynamically. Which pattern is most appropriate, and why?
options: Builder — construct the notification object before dispatching it
Chain of Responsibility — each component decides whether to handle the notification or pass it on
Observer — the notification service is the subject; components subscribe and unsubscribe dynamically without the service knowing who is listening
Decorator — wrap each component with notification-awareness
quiz.explanation: Observer: the notification service (subject) should not need to know which components are listening. Components register interest via subscribe() and deregister via unsubscribe() when unmounted. When an event fires, the service notifies all current subscribers. The key requirements — variable number of dependents, dynamic add/remove, subject unaware of dependents — are exactly what Observer is designed for.
